title: Skin for Skin: The Second Test
summary: In a second heavenly scene the LORD again points to Job's integrity, and the accuser argues that a man will give anything to save his own life. Permitted to strike Job's body but not to take his life, the accuser covers him with painful sores, and Job sits in the ashes scraping himself with broken pottery. His wife urges him to curse God and die, but he refuses; then his three friends arrive and sit with him in silence for seven days.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Job's great act of worship and the narrator's verdict that he did not sin. The accuser's first charge has failed. Now the stakes rise: having lost his possessions and children, Job will lose his health and his standing, and even his wife will turn against his faith. This chapter completes the prose prologue and introduces the three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, who will speak for most of the book. Their seven days of silence close the prologue; in chapter 3 Job will open his mouth, and the tone of the book will change completely.
historical:
Nothing in the chapter can be dated, and the setting remains the world east of Israel. The friends come from places with Edomite and Arabian connections. Eliphaz is a Temanite; Teman was a clan and region of Edom named for a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11), and Edom was known for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7). Bildad is a Shuhite; Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2), whose descendants lived in the east. Zophar is a Naamathite, from a place that has not been identified with certainty. That the friends travel from their own homes and arrange to meet suggests some time passed between Job's disasters and their arrival.

The exact nature of Job's disease is not described in medical terms. The word used for his sores is the same used of the boils of Egypt (Exodus 9:9) and of the skin disease threatened in Deuteronomy 28:35, which covers a person from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head. Later chapters mention further symptoms (7:5; 30:30), but attempts to identify a modern diagnosis are speculation.
cultural:
Sitting among the ashes, or on an ash heap, was a place of mourning and of social exclusion. Outside many ancient towns lay a dump where refuse was burned, and those who were unclean, diseased, or outcast might sit there. A man who was once the greatest in the East now sits where the lowest sit. Scraping his sores with a potsherd shows both his pain and his isolation.

The friends' response follows the customs of grief. They weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust over their heads toward the sky, symbolic acts of mourning. Sitting with a mourner for seven days recalls the seven days of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10), a practice later continued in Jewish tradition. Their silence was a mark of respect: in some later Jewish customs, visitors to a mourner were expected to wait for the mourner to speak first. Whatever their later failures, the friends' first act is compassionate.
literary: The chapter repeats the pattern of chapter 1 almost word for word in its heavenly scene, which makes the differences stand out. The LORD adds a new line: Job still holds on to his integrity, although you incited me against him without cause. The accuser's proverb, skin for skin, is obscure, but its point is clear: people will give up anything to save themselves. The limit on his power is narrower now (spare his life). Job's wife speaks one sentence, and Job answers with one question that summarizes the book's challenge: should we accept only good from God and not adversity? The narrator's verdict changes slightly from 1:22, noting that Job did not sin in what he said, literally with his lips; some interpreters see in this a hint that inner turmoil is beginning, though others think the phrase simply marks his speech as blameless.

outline.t: The second scene in the heavenly court
The three friends arrive and sit in silence

doctrines.note: Job's suffering now reaches his body and his closest relationships. The chapter refuses to separate faith from the physical reality of pain, and it lets Job's question stand: should we accept only good from God and not adversity?
Again the accuser's power is limited by God, who permits the test but forbids taking Job's life. The book holds that God rules over evil without being its author, while leaving much unexplained.
Job's integrity holds even when his wife advises him to give up. His faith is not a denial of suffering but a refusal to let suffering define God.

words.note: Tummah, integrity, wholeness. The word appears in Job more than anywhere else. The LORD says Job holds fast to his integrity, and Job's wife asks whether he still holds it. The whole debate of the book is about whether his integrity is real and whether it can survive.

Naval, foolish. Job says his wife speaks like one of the foolish women. In the Old Testament the naval is not merely unintelligent but morally and spiritually senseless, someone who acts as though God does not matter. Job doesn't call his wife a fool, but says her advice sounds like such a person's.

Nacham, to comfort, console, or show sympathy. The friends come to sympathize with Job and comfort him. The word will return with irony in 16:2, when Job calls them miserable comforters. Their first comfort is silent presence.

Barakh, to bless, used here again as a euphemism for curse. Job's wife tells him literally to bless God and die, meaning curse him. The accuser's prediction that Job would curse God is placed in the mouth of the person closest to him.

christ: Job sits among the ashes as an innocent sufferer whose closest companions misunderstand him. The book does not predict Christ, but it raises the question of a God who allows the righteous to suffer, and the New Testament answers it in part by showing God himself entering suffering in Jesus. Christ suffered in body as well as in spirit, was tested beyond all others, and was hated, as he himself said quoting the Psalms, “without reason” (John 15:25). The letter to the Hebrews says, “Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). The friends' seven days of silent presence also point toward the incarnation, God coming to sit where sufferers sit.

hard.q: Is Job's wife wicked, or is she a grieving mother?
hard.a: Job's wife is often read harshly, as the accuser's tool, because she urges Job to do exactly what the accuser predicted. Many interpreters in the church's history took this view. But she had lost her ten children and her livelihood too, and now watched her husband waste away. Many readers see her words as despair, perhaps even as a wish that his suffering would end, rather than malice. Job's reply is firm but not contemptuous: she speaks like a foolish woman, not she is one. The ancient Greek translation expands her speech into a lament for her own losses and wanderings, showing that early readers also felt the weight of her grief. She disappears from the story, though Job later says that his breath is repulsive to her (19:17). Both readings take her words seriously; the more compassionate one also takes her suffering seriously.

questions: The friends' first act is to sit silently with Job for seven days. Why is presence sometimes more helpful than words?
Job asks, should we accept good from God and not adversity? How do you respond when you feel entitled only to good?
Job's wife speaks out of grief. How can you respond with compassion to someone whose pain leads them to say hard things about God?
